kinlessness.citation: Margolis and Verdery (2017), Older Adults Without Close Kin in the United States, Journals of Gerontology Series B 72(4), Table 1: Health and Retirement Study 1998-2010, respondents 55 and older, percent with no living biological child, no living sibling, no living parent and no partner or spouse (the table's "No partner or spouse" row, since the game's couples include unmarried partners), by age group and sex.

nearKin.citation: Choi, Schoeni, Wiemers, Hotz and Seltzer (2020), Spatial Distance Between Parents and Adult Children in the United States, Journal of Marriage and Family 82(2), PSID 2013: adults with a living parent or adult child who live in a different household.
nearKin.proxy: The game places relatives by county, not by distance: a relative in the household's county stands in for one within 30 miles.

householdShape.citation: U.S. Census Bureau, American Community Survey 2020-2024 tables B11001 and B11003 for the place, else its state, as read by src/simulation/household-mix.ts.

networkTurnover.citation: Mollenhorst, Volker and Flap (2014), Social Networks 37, 65-80 (Dutch panel, 1,007 adults aged 18-65, 604 re-interviewed seven years later): 48% of the discussion partners and practical helpers named at the start were still in the network seven years later, and 30% held the same position (figures as reported in the Utrecht University release of May 27, 2009, ScienceDaily 090527111907; the 2014 article is paywalled and no kin/non-kin split was found in the sources read). The game's share of ties still above their opening closeness after seven years is compared with it in a seven-year run.
